newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Indonesian film industry hopes pinned on blockbuster.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Indonesian film industry hopes pinned on blockbuster.

text.p: Indonesia hopes a 16th-century Islamic cleric will prove a saviour to the country's neglected film industry, which is under siege from imports of slick foreign movies.
The eponymous film "Fatahillah" tells the story of a national hero who crushed a Portuguese colonial attempt to establish a trading post on Java.
At $1.24 million, it is the most expensive movie ever made in Indonesia and was released in June amid hopes it would breathe life into the country's ailing film industry.

Jakarta Governor Surjadi Soedirdja provided three billion rupiah ($1.24 million) in public funds to make the two-hour epic directed by Chaerul Umam and Imam Tantowi in celebration of the 470th birthday of Indonesia's capital.

Indonesian Minister of Education and Culture Wardiman Djojonegoro hailed the movie, which premiered on June 11, as an effort that could revive a film industry that turns out mostly low-quality slapstick and soft porn.
"What has been done by the Jakarta governor in producing the film is a valuable encouragement in awakening national film," Djojonegoro was quoted as saying this month.
The movie, which newspaper reports said was released on June 20 to modest-sized audiences, will later have further scenes added and be re-cut as a 13-part television series.
But Indonesian film observers say Fatahillah is unlikely to resurrect a backward industry constrained by political, economic and human resources problems.
"The revival isn't here yet," one movie-goer, who asked not to be named, said after the film's premiere in early June.
ONE FILM DOES NOT A REVIVAL MAKE
Indonesian film director Eros Djarot, while praising the Jakarta governor for sponsoring the film, nonetheless described it as an inadequate "hit-and-run policy".

"They are dreaming if they believe Fatahillah will be able to resurrect the Indonesian film industry. I don't believe one film can solve the problems we are facing," Djarot, director of the highly-acclaimed 1989 historic epic "Cut Nyak Dien", told Reuters.
Salim Said, film critic and chairman of The Jakarta Arts Council, echoed Djarot's opinion.

"I don't belong to the optimistic camp because this kind of shock, making a big film, has been tried several times in the last 30 years, but the Indonesian film industry is like an airplane that can not maintain its altitude," he said.
INDONESIAN FILMS UNDER SIEGE

When the United States forced open the Indonesian film industry with the threat of trade sanctions in the 1980s, film makers said the industry was not ready to match Hollywood in terms of quality, capital or human resources.
"Our films cannot compete with imported films whether it is American, Hong Kong or even Indian films," Said said.

Umam and Djarot, former editor of the banned Detik weekly, said the creativity of Indonesian film makers could not be fully explored while restrictions on freedom of expression still existed in Indonesia's tightly controlled media.

"It is true that is safer to make historical films. There are contemporary films we would like to make but we fear we might be refused permission so we have not yet asked," Uman said, citing the Indonesia's biggest-ever banking fraud case as one example of a taboo story.
BIG GAP BETWEEN MOVIE-GOERS
In addition, Indonesian movie houses are split between the haves and the have-nots, preventing a coordinated effort to revive the local industry.
A national monopoly chain owned by a relative of President Suharto shows mostly Hollywood blockbusters in sophisticated cinemas with the latest digital sound systems and deep plush seats.
Cinema-goers pay around 10,000 rupiah ($4.12), almost twice the minimum daily wage in the capital, to watch the latest releases and award-winning movies from the United States.

At the other end of the spectrum, most of Indonesia's roughly 3,000 cinemas are small smoky dens where patrons pay as little as 700 rupiah (29 cents) in the provinces to sit on hard boards to see B-grade action films from Hollywood or Hong Kong.
The locally-made films that screen in these cinemas have titles such as "Drooling over Sex", "Ecstasy and Sexuality", "Forbidden Scandal" and "Wanton Girl," leaving little doubt about the content.

Said told Reuters in an interview that any attempt by local film makers to start a new era of quality local productions is doomed as the elite do not watch locally made films and it is unprofitable to make such films for the masses.
HIGH RISKS BUT NO REWARDS
Banks will not lend money to such high-risk prospects, distributors do not return the profits to producers and high taxes on tickets of up to 33 percent make it difficult to recoup costs.

Even if the films could be financed, the equipment would have to be hired from abroad. Skilled actors, directors, writers and technicians familiar with the latest techniques are unavailable as film schools do not exist.
Said believes Indonesians need to be taught to appreciate good film, just as they are taught at school to appreciate other arts.
"Indonesia film has been about escapism since its beginning. Films about our real problems could not be appreciated by the people as they are accustomed to watching escapism," he said.
